newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Zinc fundamentals intact despite fall - dealers.
newsitem.headline: Zinc fundamentals intact despite fall - dealers.

text.p: Fundamentals in the zinc market remain intact despite a sharp fall in the metal's price, Australian metal dealers said on Wednesday.
Steady demand for zinc from the galvanising and other industries have left supply and demand in relative balance, they said.

The rout that shaved around 20 percent off the benchmark London Metal Exchange (LME) price on Tuesday was founded in a trading foul-up that left at least one big bank holding too much zinc, the dealer said.
"The seller said to the bank 'I'll take you on the bid' then sold it," one dealer said.
"Then the bank got left holding the baby for 2,000 lots of zinc expecting they would be selling it to a fund. But they ended up buying it out of their market and then tried to unload it."
Another dealer said that eventually it became apparent in the market that the lots of zinc were being jobbed around, first to buy and then to sell, and the price of zinc began to plummet.
"What happened then was it started triggering stops on the way down ... creating your typical stop-loss spiral," the dealer said.
The spread between the cash and three-month price remained relatively firm on Tuesday, suggesting some solidness in the fundamentals of the market, dealers agreed.
Little zinc concentrate from Australia is being made available on the spot market, with most material earmarked for long-term contract sales.
"A lot of people are looking at this as just an unlucky correction," a dealer in Sydney said.

Reasonably good volumes off the low points in the price, which lifted the price about US$100 a tonne, and hefty lending on the forward contracts further indicating the physical market remained on solid footing.

"Technically, zinc was very overbought ... an RSI (relative strength index) which spent a month over 70 percent and then in last couple of days went to 85 to 90 percent, would point to a buy signal," a dealer said.
However, any reemergence of "nervous shorts" in the Wednesday session could send zinc prices down again, the dealer added.
Zinc prices had climbed to around a seven-year high of US$1,700 a tonne, mainly on the back of Chinese short positions in the market.
The price came down nearly US$300 a tonne in the first hour of trading at the LME on Tuesday.
